about.label: About Me
about.p1: I'm Mohamed Khalil, a front-end developer from Egypt. I build with React, JavaScript, TypeScript, and CSS. Most of my focus goes into making interfaces that work well on any screen and don't get in the user's way.
about.p2: I completed the DEPI React Front-End Developer track and built several projects along the way: an e-commerce app, a weather app, and DevFolio. Honestly, I learned more from debugging those than from any course.
about.p3: Since January 2026 I've been a front-end intern at CASCOTEC, working on iCasco, a certification management platform built with React, Vite and TypeScript, with full Arabic/English (RTL/LTR) support. I've built pages from scratch, written the form-validation logic, turned Figma mobile designs into reusable components, and audited the platform's 22 API endpoints.

ecommerce.idea: I wanted a project that goes beyond static pages: accounts, a cart that survives navigation, and a real checkout flow. An online store forces you to solve what every serious front-end app faces — authentication, shared state, private pages, forms and a REST API. The data comes from a public practice API, so no real orders are placed.
ecommerce.role: Solo project. I planned the screens, routes and state, wrote all of the React code, styled it and deployed it.

challenges.title: A cart count that is always right
challenges.body: The cart badge in the navbar has to match the cart page, even after adding a product from another page. Instead of passing counts around, I put every cart action in one CartContext. Add, update, remove and load all read the item count from the API response and update the shared state, so the badge changes in exactly one place.

challenges.title: Keeping private pages private
challenges.body: Cart, orders and checkout must not open for a signed-out visitor. I wrapped those routes in a ProtectedRoutes component that checks the saved token and redirects to the sign-in page, so the rule is written once instead of in every page.

challenges.title: Brands from a paginated API
challenges.body: The brands endpoint returns data page by page. I loop until the last page, then run the search box and the A–Z filter in the browser, so filtering feels instant.

decisions.title: React 19, Vite and React Router 7
decisions.body: Vite gives instant feedback while building. The router's nested layouts let the navbar and footer exist once, while sign-in and sign-up use their own layout.

decisions.title: Context API instead of Redux
decisions.body: Only two things are truly global here: the signed-in user and the cart. Context covers that without another library. I would reach for a state library only if the app grew.

decisions.title: Formik and Yup for forms
decisions.body: Sign-up and sign-in need clear validation messages. Formik tracks values and touched fields, and Yup keeps the rules in a readable schema.

decisions.title: A hosted payment page
decisions.body: Checkout collects the shipping details and sends the visitor to the payment page created by the API, so payment details never pass through my code.

outcome: A complete shopping flow: sign up, sign in, browse products, view details, manage the cart, check out and view orders.
A responsive layout built on Bootstrap's grid, with a CSS module for every component.
Live and deployed, with the code public on GitHub.
ecommerce.learned: Planning the data flow first made everything else simpler. Looking back, I would change three things: create one Axios instance that reads the token on every request (today it is read when the file loads, so it can be stale until a refresh after signing in), move server data to TanStack Query for caching and loading states, and connect the orders screen, which currently shows sample data, to the real endpoint. I would also write it in TypeScript, which is what I used for this portfolio.

velora.idea: Velora is a landing page for a fictional premium organic coffee brand. I wanted to practice what makes a marketing page feel alive — storytelling sections, product cards, motion on scroll — and to do it in Arabic, fully right-to-left, using only HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript.
velora.role: Solo project: layout, Arabic copy, styling and all the JavaScript, with no framework.

challenges.title: Designing for right-to-left
challenges.body: The page is Arabic from the root: <html lang="ar" dir="rtl">. Setting the direction once on the root element made text and layout flow right-to-left, and I then checked every section for spacing, icons and slider direction instead of patching them one by one.

challenges.title: Many scroll animations, one pattern
challenges.body: Each section reveals itself when it enters the screen. I used IntersectionObserver rather than scroll listeners, so the browser tells me when something is visible. The stats counters use the same idea: they count up from zero only when the row appears, then stop observing.

challenges.title: A navbar that knows where you are
challenges.body: A scroll-spy highlights the link of the section you are reading and smooth-scrolls when a link is clicked, which makes a single long page easy to navigate.

decisions.title: No framework
decisions.body: A brand landing page has no complex state. Plain JavaScript keeps it light and let me practice the browser APIs underneath frameworks.

decisions.title: Bootstrap 5 for the grid
decisions.body: I used it for the responsive grid and the navbar and wrote the visual identity — colours, cards, hero — in my own CSS.

decisions.title: Swiper for the testimonials
decisions.body: A touch-friendly slider with autoplay and clickable pagination, instead of building one from scratch.

outcome: A seven-section responsive Arabic landing page: hero, story, products, features, testimonials, call to action and footer.
Scroll-triggered animations, animated counters, a scroll-spy navbar and a testimonials slider.
Live on GitHub Pages with the code public.
velora.learned: This project taught me how much work lives in the details of animation timing and RTL. If I rebuilt it today I would share one reveal helper across every section instead of one observer per block, and respect reduced-motion settings.

qr.idea: A one-screen landing page for a QR-code product, built to practice a polished first impression: a bold hero, subtle depth, and an endless strip of partner logos that signals trust.
qr.role: Solo project: design, HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

challenges.title: A seamless logo marquee
challenges.body: The partner strip scrolls forever with no visible jump. The logos are duplicated and the track moves by exactly half of its width, so the loop restarts invisibly. It pauses on hover, and soft fades on both edges hide where logos enter and leave.

challenges.title: Depth without heaviness
challenges.body: The hero content drifts slightly slower than the scroll for a parallax feel, using a passive scroll listener so scrolling is never blocked. Sections fade up once through IntersectionObserver.

decisions.title: CSS for motion, JavaScript only where needed
decisions.body: The marquee, hero entrance and glow are CSS animations, which the browser can run smoothly. JavaScript only decides when something becomes visible.

decisions.title: Bootstrap for responsiveness
decisions.body: Spacing and breakpoints are tuned in the stylesheet so the marquee and cards stay balanced on phones.

outcome: A focused, fast landing page with a hero entrance, parallax, scroll reveals and an infinite marquee.
Responsive on phone, tablet and desktop.
Live on Vercel with the code public.
qr.learned: Small, well-timed animation does more for perceived quality than many effects. Next time I would add a prefers-reduced-motion fallback from the start and compress the logo images further.

alex.idea: A portfolio for a back-end developer. The challenge was to make a back-end profile feel visual: so the hero types out a real API route, as if you were watching the developer write it.
alex.role: Solo project: structure, design, content layout and all the React code.

challenges.title: A typing animation done the React way
challenges.body: The code in the hero is typed one character at a time with a blinking cursor. State tracks the current line and character, and a timer inside useEffect advances it and is cleaned up on every step, so nothing keeps running after the component unmounts.

challenges.title: Filterable projects
challenges.body: Visitors can filter the project list by category. The filter is derived from a single piece of state and the list, so there is no duplicated data to keep in sync.

decisions.title: Sections as components
decisions.body: Hero, About, Experience, Tech Stack, Projects and Contact are separate components with their own CSS modules, so each part can change without touching the others.

decisions.title: Content kept as data
decisions.body: Projects, stats and tech tags live in arrays at the top of each file, so updating the portfolio is an edit to data, not to markup.

outcome: A responsive one-page portfolio with a typing hero, floating technology tags, an experience section, tech stack, filterable projects and a contact section.
Live on Vercel with the code public. The profile content is sample content for the design.
alex.learned: Animation timers are easy to get subtly wrong in React. This project taught me to always clean up effects. Next time I would add proper TypeScript types for the content arrays.

ahmed.idea: A clean, professional portfolio for a back-end developer, centred on the essentials a recruiter looks for: skills, experience, selected projects and an easy way to get in touch, with a one-click résumé button.
ahmed.role: Solo project: planning, design and all the React code.

challenges.title: Navigation that follows the reader
challenges.body: The navbar highlights the section currently on screen and changes style after scrolling. A scroll handler works out the active section, and the listener is removed on cleanup. On mobile, tapping a link closes the menu.

challenges.title: Keeping a simple site simple
challenges.body: With few sections it is tempting to over-build. I kept one page, one layout and small components, so the site stays fast and easy to read.

decisions.title: React with CSS Modules
decisions.body: Scoped styles per component avoid class-name clashes and make each section independent.

decisions.title: A visible résumé action
decisions.body: The résumé download sits in the navbar, where recruiters expect it.

outcome: A responsive one-page portfolio with skills, experience, projects and contact sections.
A scroll-aware navbar and a mobile menu.
Live on Vercel with the code public. The profile content is sample content for the design.
ahmed.learned: Restraint is a design decision: fewer sections made the page clearer. I would add semantic landmarks and keyboard focus styles earlier in the process.

youssef.idea: A portfolio for a web designer and software engineer with personality: a typewriter headline that alternates between the two roles, followed by skills, projects, key numbers and a contact section.
youssef.role: Solo project: design, structure and all the React code.

challenges.title: A two-role typewriter
challenges.body: The headline types one role, pauses, deletes it and types the next. It is a small state machine — typing, pausing, deleting — driven by a timer inside useEffect.

challenges.title: Showing numbers without clutter
challenges.body: A compact stats row summarises the work (projects, files, lines of code) so the page communicates scale at a glance without long paragraphs.

decisions.title: React, Bootstrap and CSS Modules
decisions.body: Bootstrap handles the responsive grid and the collapsing navbar; CSS Modules hold the custom look of each section.

decisions.title: A fixed navbar that adapts
decisions.body: It stays visible and changes its background after the page scrolls, so it never fights the hero.

outcome: A responsive one-page portfolio with a typewriter hero, about, skills, stats, projects and contact sections.
A downloadable résumé action.
Live on Vercel with the code public. The profile content is sample content for the design.
youssef.learned: Even a simple animation benefits from being modelled as states. If I rebuilt it I would pause the typewriter for reduced-motion users and replace the placeholder numbers with real ones.

weather.idea: A weather app I built during DEPI to practise HTML, CSS, JavaScript and working with a real API. It shows today's conditions and the next two days for any city, using WeatherAPI. After the first version worked I rewrote it for reliability: a search that does not hammer the API, honest error states, and a layout that works with a keyboard.
weather.role: Solo project: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, API integration, and the later rewrite for reliability and accessibility.

challenges.title: Search that fires on every keystroke
challenges.body: The first version requested a full forecast for every letter typed after the third. That wastes the API quota, and a slow response for "Alex" could arrive after the one for "Alexandria" and overwrite it. Typing now only fetches suggestions, debounced by 300 ms, and every request cancels the previous one with AbortController, so the latest request always wins.

challenges.title: Everything that can go wrong with a network call
challenges.body: A city that does not exist, a lost connection, a slow server and an exhausted quota all used to leave the page frozen on the previous result. Requests now time out after 10 seconds, WeatherAPI error codes map to plain-language messages with a Try again button, and when the network fails the app shows the last saved forecast for that city with a clear warning.

challenges.title: An API key that ended up on GitHub
challenges.body: The first version had the key written straight into the script and pushed to a public repository. I moved it into a config file that is not committed, generate that file from an environment variable in the Vercel build step, and rotated the exposed key. The main lesson is that any key used in browser JavaScript is visible to visitors, so a front-end key must be low-value and replaceable.

challenges.title: Dates that showed the wrong weekday
challenges.body: Parsing a date-only string such as 2026-10-11 with new Date() treats it as UTC, so viewers west of UTC could see the previous day. The forecast date already belongs to the city, so it is now formatted as-is, without shifting it by the viewer's time zone.

decisions.title: Shape the API response before rendering
decisions.body: The raw payload is validated and reduced to a small model with only the fields the UI uses. If something is missing, the app reports a readable error instead of crashing halfway through updating the screen.

decisions.title: Write API text with textContent, never innerHTML
decisions.body: City names and conditions come from an external service, so they are inserted as plain text. Icon URLs are only accepted from WeatherAPI's own CDN, with a local fallback icon if one fails to load.

decisions.title: Both units from one response
decisions.body: WeatherAPI returns Celsius and Fahrenheit together, so switching units only re-renders the data already on the page. The choice and the last city are remembered between visits.

decisions.title: Ask for location only when the user taps the button
decisions.body: A permission prompt on page load is intrusive and easy to dismiss by reflex. The Use my location button asks at the moment the user wants it, and a denial shows a clear message and leaves search available.

outcome: A working three-day forecast with live suggestions, a °C/°F toggle and remembered settings.
Reliable under failure: timeouts, cancelled stale requests, readable errors and a saved-forecast fallback.
Keyboard-operable search (combobox pattern), labelled controls, visible focus and reduced-motion support.
The background image went from 12.6 MB to 354 KB, and the page no longer loads Font Awesome or Google Fonts.
Live on Vercel with the code public.
weather.learned: Most of the work in a small API app is not the happy path, it is cancelled requests, error messages and bad data. Next I would add unit tests for the data-shaping and formatting functions, and put the API key behind a tiny serverless proxy so it is not exposed to the browser at all.
